    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Andoni Iraola has conceded that Liverpool cannot currently “sustain the level” he expects after his side squandered a two-goal lead for the second match in a row.
    • In the Spaniard’s first game at Anfield since becoming manager, Monaco fought back to win 3-2 by virtue of Paris Brunner’s late glancing header seven days on from Leeds United’s 4-2 victory in Chicago, emphasising Liverpool’s alarming lack of depth, particularly in defence.
    • Industry observers note that “We played a good first half, especially a good 30 minutes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Andoni Iraola has conceded that Liverpool cannot currently “sustain the level” he expects after his side squandered a two-goal lead for the second match in a row.

    In the Spaniard’s first game at Anfield since becoming manager, Monaco fought back to win 3-2 by virtue of Paris Brunner’s late glancing header seven days on from Leeds United’s 4-2 victory in Chicago, emphasising Liverpool’s alarming lack of depth, particularly in defence.

    Industry observers note that “We played a good first half, especially a good 30 minutes. Right now we probably don’t have much more, in terms of the levels required to play like this. They deserved to turn around the game.

    “We won the first two pre-season games, but the last two we cannot sustain the level we want for all of the game. As soon as we made some changes, players start to get tired and we cannot sustain that level. So, we have work to do.”.

    Alex on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/PT6AYrLxyz.

    Alisson, Virgil van Dijk and Cody Gakpo all made their first appearances and contributed to a lively first-half in which Iraola’s commitment to man-to-man marking and an intensive pressing structure were evident out of possession. With the ball in the first half they demonstrated the kind of slick passing that Bournemouth employed to carve opponents open on the counter-attack.

    A nimble one-two between Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai allowed the Dutch midfielder to set up Alexander Isak to score with a shot from 16 yards and the most expensive player in English football history laid claim to the second, too, when he seemed to hook in a rebound from Lukas Hradecky’s save while lying in the six-yard box.

    Later he would graciously acknowledge that he and Florian Wirtz had connected with the ball simultaneously and he was happy to yield the credit to his team-mate.

    Our second goal of the game, scored by Wirtz… we think 🤔 pic.twitter.com/FUzA363Oxw.

    Sources indicate that at that point it seemed that victory would be a cakewalk but just before half-time Aleksandr Golovin caught Van Dijk out with a feint and late swerve to the right, tripping over the Liverpool captain’s clumsy hack. Despite a heavy limp, Golovin hammered the penalty past Alisson’s dive to make it 2-1 at the break.

    Iraola rationed his early changes at the start of the second half to two but Liverpool could not regain their rhythm and Mika Biereth capitalised on a Gravenberch error to score the equaliser after battling to be first to the rebound when Giorgi Mamardashvili saved his first effort, stroking his effort through Wataru Endo’s legs.

    Cue five substitutions as soon as that goal had gone in and a raft more followed, killing the remaining half-hour of all momentum and cohesion. By the time Brunner exploited a dozy mix-up between Milos Kerkez and Federico Chiesa about whose responsibility he was at a corner to flash his header past Mamardashvili, only two of the 22 starters were still on the pitch.

    It has been revealed that liverpool: Alisson (Mamardashvili 46), Tsimikas (Kerkez 59), Van Dijk (c) (Chambers 59), Ndukwe (Endo 46), Frimpong (Ramsay 75), Gravenberch (Nyoni 59), Gakpo (Ngumoha 59), Wirtz (McConnell 59), Koumas (Chiesa 75), Isak (Muñoz 59)Substitutes: Morrison, Davies.Goals: Isak (16), Wirtz (29)Monaco: Hradecky, Nazinho (Mawissa 75), Dier (c) (Kehrer 75), S Sané, Vanderson (Teze 46), Golovin (Idumbo 75), Cabral (Soubeir 75), Camara (Benzahra 64), Detourbet (Coulibaly 64), Biereth (Brunner 80), Abline (Konaté 64).Substitutes: Assab, Kohn, Lienard, Nibombe, Touré. Goals: Golovin (44 pen), Biereth (56), Brunner (88).

    They played well in the first half, as they did against Leeds, but lost all shape and structure in the second half to lose 3-2.

    Sources indicate that yellow card for Konate for clattering into Endo late. That’s the last of the action.

    Liverpool 2 Monaco 3 (Brunner)  Brilliant near-post glancing header from a devilishly whippy, dipping corner. Kerkez doing his best Rip van Winkle impression.

    Diligent defensive work by Ngumoha stops Konate’s run down the outside left.

    A final substitution, hopefully. Brunner replaces Biereth. Konate’s shot, a pearoller, is easily saved by Mamardashvili after A mix-up between Kerkez and Munoz.

    As usual, the substitutions have killed the game. Watched Leeds vs RB Leipzig yesterday. They played two 60 minute matches which kept it more competitive for longer but still descended into a kickabout late on.

    Mawissa, Kehrer, Idumbo and Soubeir have replaced Nazinho, Dier, Golovin and Cabral.

    Industry observers note that monaco also made changes, four I think. Will catch up with then once they’re confirmed. Ramsey is into the game straight away tp stop Coulibaly’s shot.

    Industry observers note that ramsay, Chiesa and Elliott are coming on for Szoboszlai, Frimpong and Koumas. Lovely applause for Elliott.

    It has been revealed that konate sweeps a left-foot shot from the left of the box past the right post with Mamardashvili forced into a headlong dive. Liverpool have lost their defensive shape and intensity, allowing Monaco to punch holes through the lines with some direct running.

    Recent findings suggest that nazinho gets round Frimpong down the Monaco left and cuts back the perfect pass to put it on a plate for Coulibaly who hammers a left-foot shot from the right of the D that Mamardashvili throws up his hands to block. That would have stung. Good save. A flag would have meant it wouldn’t have counted but even so Frimpong’s defensive work wasn’t good enough.

    Industry observers note that it’s been very scrappy since the changes but then Ngumoha pounces on to a loose ball, glides up the right and tries to play Koumas in behind the back four. Sadly, he overhits the pass which trickles out for a goal-kick. Cue an ovation and cries of ‘Rio! Rio!’.

    Three changes for Monaco with Detoubet, Abline and Camara departing for Benzhara, Coulibaly and Konaté.

    Ngumoha has gone to the right wing and Koumas is playing through the middle as a false nine.

    Liverpool make five changes with Gakpo, Van Dijk, Wirtz, Tsimikas and Isak departing while Munoz makes his ‘debut’ with Ngumoha, Nyoni, Chambers, McConell and Kerkez.

    According to recent reports, liverpool 2 Monaco 2 (Biereth) Mistake by Gravenberch allows Golovin to play a pass into the left half of the box for Biereth. His first shot is well saved by Mamardashvili at full stretch but his tenacity allowed him to get to the rebound ahead of Endo, swivel and stick his second effort in to equalise.

    Industry observers note that monaco overplay at the edge of the box, Detourbet, Biereth and Abline playing ‘after you. Claud’, instead of shooting.

    A slick, short passing move between Gravenberch, Wirtz and Isak ends with Isak on the deck in the box after Gravenberch’s step-over allowed the ball to run to him. Isak took a touch to move the ball on to his left but gave the defender a glimmer of it and he hacked it away before felling Isak as well as collateral damage.

    Quiet start to the half. Biereth just pressed Mamardashvili but the keeper managed to sweep the ball away even though under more pressure than he would have expected.

    Liverpool try to play out from the back with Mamardashvili spearing a straight pass to Gravenberch who tried to knock it round the corner for Endo but the ball skidded under his studs and out for a throw-in.

The man-to-man system is working well for them. But they should be out of sight by now instead of leading by only a goal.

    Liverpool free-kick on the right after a foul on Koumas. Szoboszlai whips in the cross and Van Dijk gets up first to the left of the penalty spot but bludgeons his header about a foot wide of the right post.

    Charlie Adam claims the penalty was ‘a soft one’ but Van Dijk did not adjust when Golovin shifted it to his right, stuck out a leg and Golovim understandably decided to topple over the hurdle.

    Liverpool 2 Monaco 1 (Golovin, pen) Speared it into the top right. Alisson went the right way but was beaten for pace and power.

    According to recent reports, the referee, Jarred Gillett, gives Monaco a penalty. It was deserved, too. Golovin went on a driving run down the middle, shifted it to his right and was tripped by Van Dijk.

    Liverpool are well worth their lead. They are streets ahead of Monaco.

    A microcosm of the game so far: Liverpool pass goes astray, a player wins it back – this time Gakpo – by snapping into a tackle before laying it off to his left for the unmarked Tsimikas to skim a low shot about a foot wide of the left post from 25 yards.

    Monaco have done very little since that wee salvo in the opening minute but just now Abline was given too much space from distance but whacked his shot into the Kop.

    Massive cheer from the crowd for Hugo Ekitike.

    The impressive Koumas diddles Nazinho with a Cruyff turn but then thumps his shot straight into Hradecky’s chest.

    In a recent development, liverpool 2 Monaco 0 (Wirtz) Pass chipped out to Koumas down the right who arcs a cross to the back post. Gakpo meets it with a header back across goal to Isak whose first effort from a couple of yards is blocked but the ball gets stuck under Isak’s falling body and Wirtz is Johnny on the Spot to stab it in from a 18 inches as Dier tried to scramble it away.

    Liverpool have been impressive so far but if there has been a weakness it’s still the balance in central midfield defensively. Going forward both Gravenberch and Szobiszlai have dovetailed together well. They win the ball back when Van Dijk steps out and the midfield two fly forward to tee up Koumas for a shot that strikes Dier.

    Chance for Wirtz, who opens his body from the left of the D to try to bend a shot into the bottom right corner but fizzes it the wrong side of the post.

    Ifeanyi Ndukwe, who played well in America after coming on for the injured Joe Gomez, does not have a UK work permit and will have to go abroad on loan for the season but Jérémy Jacquet, who has yet to feature, was due to have a fitness test this morning and would be a welcome to boost to a squad whose defence still requires significant reinforcements.

    #3774. NBA MVP Rankings: Luka Dončić, Victor Wembanyama in a two-horse race; Stephen Curry's absence speaks volumes

    NBA MVP Rankings: Luka Dončić, Victor Wembanyama in a two-horse race; Stephen Curry's absence speaks volumes

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We're nearly a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while some people say it's too early to start talking about MVP, we are not among those people.
    • Right now, it's a clear two-horse race: Luka Doncic or Victor Wembanyama?
    • Sources indicate that the Luka Dončić we're watching right now isn't just the best offensive player in the world.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We're nearly a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while some people say it's too early to start talking about MVP, we are not among those people.

    Right now, it's a clear two-horse race: Luka Doncic or Victor Wembanyama? There is a real split on this. Here's where I stand as of Tuesday, Nov. 17.

    Sources indicate that the Luka Dončić we're watching right now isn't just the best offensive player in the world. He might be the best in history. Nobody has ever put up anything close to the numbers he is charting at the moment: 39 points per game with seven assists, seven boards, nearly two steals and a positively scorching 66.0 TS%, the latter being a number even the great Stephen Curry has only bested twice in his career.

    It's early, sure. Dončić isn't likely to keep making 3s at this rate for an entire season, and indeed we've seen some slippage of late (35% over his last four, if you really want to split hairs), but his volume remains, with 4.5 makes a night over that stretch. Dončić remains on track to break Curry's single-season record of 402 3-pointers, and he's done more off-ball shooting than in the past.

    Sources indicate that throw in more transition production and a 53% midrange conversion rate, per Cleaning The Glass, and you're seeing a more diverse scorer, which is to say this isn't just a guy who has started off hot on his step-back 3s (though this is a major factor, too, of course), but a guy piercing defenses from more spots with different shots. If Dončić could actually be any harder to guard than he has been in the past, we're seeing it this season.

    Sources indicate that he's also defending. His 23 steals rank sixth league-wide. Only two players have recovered more defensive loose balls than his eight. Only one has taken more charges than his four. With Dončić as the primary defender, shooters are converting just 36.7% of their shots against a 45.1 expected FG%; that minus-8.6 is the fourth-largest discrepancy among all players who've contested at least 150 shots.

    Most importantly, the Lakers are 12-2 and tied with the Spurs atop the Western Conference. The Lakers rank as the league's top offense with a rating that balloons to 129.2 points per 100 possessions (which would be an NBA record by a long shot) with Dončić on, and a net rating, as illustrated below, that falls off a cliff when he sits.

    Look, if you have Wembanyama ahead of Dončić in the MVP race a month into the season, nobody is going to argue much with you. The oddsmakers slightly favor Wembanyama (+110 at FanDuel; Dončić is +140), who, as you'll see below, has what would qualify as a potentially unanimous case in most years. But this isn't most years. We got a dude averaging nearly 40 points for a No. 1 seed that nobody expected to be a No. 1 seed. Until one of those things changes, it's hard for me to go against Dončić.

    If you think Dončić's plus-35.5 on/off split (it's actually plus-32.2 without filtering for garbage time) is crazy, have a look at Wembanyama's number.

    Victor Wembanyama's impact this season has been another level. Spurs are +42.6 points per 100 possessions with Wemby on the court than off it, according to @cleantheglass. Small sample but other-worldly. Lakers star Luka Dončić is at +35.5 pts/100 poss.Both numbers are better… pic.twitter.com/0GJCFFmZ5K.

    Yes, you're reading that right. The Spurs, for all their supportive talent, fall by 42.6 points per 100 possessions when Wembanyama leaves the court (plus-29.2 on vs. minus-13.3 off), per Cleaning the Glass. By comparison, the best on/off split that Nikola Jokić has ever recorded is plus-24.8. Curry's best is plus-21.3. LeBron James' is plus-17.8. Go down that list and look at the most impactful on-off splits those guys have ever posted. Wembanyama is in another galaxy.

    Recent findings suggest that and it's crucial to note that Wembanyama plays on a great team, as all these guys in the graphic have. The fact that there is still so much difference between when Wembanyama is on the court and when he isn't, even in a small sample, is honestly difficult to comprehend. San Antonio's three-guard lineup was supposed to be an experiment, but it's hard to know if Dylan Harper, De'Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle truly optimize one another or if Wembanyama is enough to make any lineup dominant in spite of traditional problems (like none of those three being a true shooter).

    Wembanyama is the best defensive player on the planet by an immeasurable amount. Even the stats don't do it justice. He's on pace for north of 350 blocks, a number only four players (Elmore Smith, Mark Eaton, Manute Bol and Hakeem Olajuwon) have eclipsed since blocks became an official stat in 1973, and still it's just as much, if not more, about the shots he deters scorers from even attempting.

    And why would they? Scorers are making just 33.6% of their shots when Wembanyama is the nearest defender, a 17% drop from their expected 50.4%. That also leads the league among all players who've defended at least 120 shots, and again, it fails to fully capture his defensive dominance.

    Sources indicate that the fact that we've gotten this far without talking about Wembanyama's offense, as if it's a mere afterthought for a guy to be averaging 28.6 points and 11.6 rebounds in under 30 minutes a night. Wembanyama is figuring out his hot spots, prioritizing closer-to-the-basket positioning where he is a skyscraper among regular NBA buildings. He's taking two more paint shots per game than he did last season; 43% of his shots are coming from inside four feet, per Cleaning the Glass, up from 38% last season, and his 4.6 dunks per game (up from 2.7 last year) have him on pace to shatter Rudy Gobert's single-season record of 306.

    Sources indicate that if I had to guess, Wembanyama's production is more sustainable than Dončić's. It's hard to imagine Dončić not hitting a rough patch from 3, and he's almost certainly not going to keep scoring 39 points per game. He'll be over 35 points per game when everything is said and done because that's what the Lakers need from him, but there's a burnout factor while Wembanyama is kind of cruising to these numbers, and the defensive impact is as natural as breathing. My gut notes Wembanyama will be a clearer MVP favorite by Christmas.

    Assuming Dončić and Wembanyama each get to the mandated 65 games, everyone else is playing for third place at the moment. Which is crazy given the seasons some of the following names are having.

    One of two players averaging at least 22 points, nine rebounds and seven assists, and the only player to be leading his team in all three categories. The Rockets are 11-4 with the No. 2 offense and Sengun is the center of it all.

    Sources indicate that tatum is averaging his normal 26.5 points per game. The shooting efficiency still hasn't come around, but he is an absolute quarterback on this Celtics team. He draws the doubles, and his 35.1% assist rate, per CTG, is a career high by a mile. The Celtics, for my money, are the best team in the East.

    Cunningham is, once again, doing everything for the Pistons, who have been without Jalen Duren for all but the first four games and are still a top-three East seed. The 3-point shooting is down, but that's splitting hairs. This guy is shot-creating machine and, as forceful as he plays, he makes it look as smooth as anyone in the league.

    Here come the Heat, who have won five straight games, with the last three wins coming over the Cavaliers, Pistons and Rockets. Antetokounmpo is averaging 28.3/12.5/5.2 with 1.3 blocks per game on 60% shooting. He's on fire from the midrange as the Heat are exploiting the soft spots in all the drop coverage they're facing.

    It has been revealed that gilgeous-Alexander has so much on his plate that it actually creates a clearer path to a third straight MVP if he can somehow lift Oklahoma City above all these injuries. He's trying. The Thunder are 9-5 and he's getting his 30.9 points per game, but his 58.7 true-shooting is down considerably, which makes sense as he has to force tougher shots now with fewer weapons around him.

    In a recent development, curry's value can perhaps be felt most in his absence. The Warriors have lost three straight since he went out with a torn oblique, the last two by 59 points. The Warriors have outscored opponents by 13.5 points per 100 possessions with Curry on the floor this season and have been outscored by 8.3 points per 100 possessions without him. Along with Yaxel Lendeborg, who's being asked as a rookie to carry an impossibly heavy weight without Curry, Curry remains the only real lifeblood of a team that is still shockingly lifeless without him.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the Boston Red Sox have made the offseason's first major free agent signing. The Red Sox and first baseman Jake Bauers have agreed to a four-year contract worth a reported $58 million, the team confirmed on Tuesday.

    In a recent development, bauers, 31, broke out with the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers this past season, authoring a .266/.389/.484 batting line with 26 home runs that more than doubled his previous career high (12).     💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that two players have accepted this year's one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer prior to Tuesday's 4 p.m.
    • An eighth free agent, Jake Bauers, also received the QO.
    • It has been revealed that the five unsigned free agents who rejected the QO are now tied to draft pick compensation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that two players have accepted this year's one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer prior to Tuesday's 4 p.m. ET. deadline, and six others have declined the QO. David Bednar (Yankees) and Ryan Jeffers (Twins) are returning to their teams, for the 2027 season, while Randy Arozarena (Mariners),  Brandon Lowe (Pirates), Adrian Morejon (Padres), Trevor Rogers (Orioles), and Seiya Suzuki (Cubs) are all hitting the market.

    An eighth free agent, Jake Bauers, also received the QO. He agreed to a four-year, $58 million contract with the Red Sox this past weekend. Effectively, Bauers declined the QO. Because they paid CBT in 2026, the Red Sox will surrender their second- and fifth-highest 2027 draft picks, plus $1 million in 2027 international bonus pool money, to sign Bauers. The Brewers, as a revenue-sharing receiver, will receive a compensation draft pick after the first round because the contract exceeds $50 million.

    It has been revealed that the five unsigned free agents who rejected the QO are now tied to draft pick compensation. Their former teams will receive a draft pick if they sign elsewhere, and their latest teams will be docked a draft pick and potentially international bonus pool money to sign them. The exact compensation depends on the team's revenue sharing and competitive balance tax (CBT) status.

    Here is draft pick compensation the former teams will receive if the seven qualified free agents change teams:.

    Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round) if contract under $50M; pick after first round if over $50M.

    Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round) if contract under $50M; pick after first round if over $50M.

    Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round) if contract under $50M; pick after first round if over $50M.

    According to recent reports, CBT payors, like the Red Sox, will forfeit their second- and fifth-highest 2027 draft picks, plus $1 million in 2027 international bonus pool money, to sign a qualified free agent. Teams that receive revenue sharing will surrender their third-highest 2027 draft pick. All other teams will surrender their second-highest 2027 draft pick and $500,000 in 2027 international bonus pool money.

    In a recent development, it must be noted that declining the QO does not mean the free agent can not return to his former team. The two sides could still work out a contract of any size and any length, including one worth less than QO, though that is very unlikely. Zac Gallen, Michael King, and Kyle Schwarber rejected the QO last offseason and then later re-signed with their teams.

    It has been revealed that free agents must meet certain criteria to be eligible for the QO. Players cannot have received the QO previously and they must have spent the most recent season with one team, meaning anyone traded in-season is ineligible. The Dodgers could not give Tarik Skubal, far and away the offseason's best free agent, the QO following his midseason acquisition.

    Sources indicate that the QO is set at the average of the top 125 salaries in the most recent season and that is salaries only, not total compensation. For example, the Yankees paid Cody Bellinger a $20 million signing bonus and a $32.5 million salary in 2026. Only the $32.5 million counts toward the QO calculation. This QO was worth a record $23.15 million this winter.

    It has been revealed that the current QO system replaced the old free-agent arbitration system in 2012 and will remain in effect this offseason. The upcoming collective bargaining agreement could change the QO system, if not eliminate it entirely. Entering the offseason, just 18 of the 157 free agents to receive the QO accepted it. That count is now at 20 of 165.

    One of the more effective closers in baseball last season, Bednar closed down 35 of 39 save chances with a 2.47 ERA, 1.04 WHIP and 76 strikeouts in 69 ⅓ innings. Having him back on board means the Yankees don't need to find a new closer and can look instead to shore up the bridge to the ninth as needed.

    Sources indicate that there had been talk that Jeffers wanted to stay with the Twins but that he'd decline the QO and then negotiate a long-term deal. There's still room to reach an extension, of course, but he now doesn't have any leverage from outside offers. It's a significant win for the Twins, with Jeffers resuming his role as the everyday catcher and Victor Caratini serving as the primary backup.

    Recent findings suggest that jeffers hit .256/.353/.461 (127 OPS+) with 14 homers and 56 RBI is only 92 games last season. He's been one of the most productive offensive catchers in baseball over the course of the last four seasons, when healthy.

    Arsenal suffered back-to-back pre-season defeats as they lost 3-2 to Borussia Dortmund in the Emirates Cup on Sunday.

    The loss to the German side followed a 3-1 defeat by Real Betis on Wednesday night in Dublin.

    Before kick-off, Bruno Guimarães was paraded to the Arsenal faithful after completing his £75m move from Newcastle on Saturday.

    But enthusiasm about the Brazilian’s arrival was dampened when Dortmund took the lead at the Emirates inside the opening 10 minutes. Felix Nmecha’s incisive pass into the penalty area was met by the run of Samuele Inácio, who made no mistake with a clinical finish into the far corner.

    The Bundesliga side doubled their lead just before the half-hour mark as 18-year-old Greek international Konstantinos Karetsas curled one in from the edge of the box.

    Ten minutes after half-time, Arsenal pulled a goal back through Ethan Nwaneri, who scored from Christos Tzolis’s cross. However, moments later Dortmund restored their two-goal advantage as Joane Gadou smashed home from a corner.

    Arsenal kept their hopes alive through a Viktor Gyokeres penalty after Tzolis was brought down, but Dortmund were able to hold on to claim victory. After the full-time whistle, there was a penalty shoot-out, which Arsenal won 5-4.

    Arsenal still have a number of players to return to action following their World Cup exploits, including Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Noni Madueke. England and Real Madrid midfielder Jude Bellingham was in attendance at the Emirates to watch his younger brother Jobe in action for Dortmund.

    Premier League champions Arsenal continue their preparations for the new season as they take on Borussia Dortmund in the Emirates Cup. Arsenal beat Spanish side Athletic Bilbao 3-0 in the 2025 edition, with goals from Viktor Gyokeres, Bukayo Saka and Kai Havertz sealing victory. These sides met during the 2014/15 Champions League group stages, with both games being won 2-0 by the home side.

    Arsenal beat Girona 4-1 just over a week ago but fell to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night. Reflecting on that defeat, Mikel Arteta expressed his frustration at the way his side conceded the goals.

    Recent findings suggest that “I am disappointed with the result,” Arteta told Arsenal’s in-house media. “We are here to win football matches. We had some fantastic moments in the first half, the way we played, the way we opened them up. We have to score first, clearly, in the two chances that we had before the score.

    It has been revealed that “I am very disappointed in the manner that we conceded the first goal, the two giveaways leading to the other two goals. It is true that the finishing quality from them was exceptional, but to win a football match, you have to compete at a different level, especially in those areas of the pitch and that is the learning from today [last Wednesday].”.

    Sources indicate that this is in fact Arsenal’s first game at the Emirates since being crowned Premier League champions, as they sealed the title with a game to spare, with that final match of last season being away at Crystal Palace. After today, Arsenal have two more games, including the Community Shield in a week’s time, before they kick off the defence of their Premier League crown at home against newly-promoted Coventry. The likes of Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Martin Zubimendi are still yet to return after their World Cup exploits.

    Recent findings suggest that dortmund, led by Niko Kovac, finished second in the Bundesliga last season, 16 points off winners Bayern Munich. They have played four pre-season friendlies thus far, winning twice and losing twice. The likes of Karim Adeyemi, Julian Brandt and Niklas Sule have left the club this summer.

    #3765. Re-grading the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade: Why the Heat and Bucks both look much worse now

    Re-grading the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade: Why the Heat and Bucks both look much worse now

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2338 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Giannis Antetokounmpo will face the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time as an opponent on Wednesday, but it's a game that feels as though it's a half-decade or more in the making.
    • Sources indicate that the Bucks kept kicking the can down the road.
    • Industry observers note that now, Antetokounmpo plays for the Heat while the Bucks are in no man's land.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Giannis Antetokounmpo will face the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time as an opponent on Wednesday, but it's a game that feels as though it's a half-decade or more in the making. The Miami Heat were a rumored suitor for Antetokounmpo, who played his first 13 NBA seasons in Milwaukee, as far back as the buildup to his possible 2021 free agency, which the Bucks averted by trading for Jrue Holiday and ultimately winning a championship.

    Sources indicate that the Bucks kept kicking the can down the road. They secured another extension with Antetokounmpo in 2023 by trading for Damian Lillard. They stuck their fingers in their ears and pretended everything was fine when Lillard tore his Achilles in 2025, in the process bypassing the chance to trade Antetokounmpo with multiple years left on his contract when they could have maximized his trade value. In the end, though, Heat president Pat Riley did what he has done so many times before: he got his man.

    Industry observers note that now, Antetokounmpo plays for the Heat while the Bucks are in no man's land. We have around four weeks of data on how these teams are going to look after one of the bigger blockbusters in recent NBA history, so with their first head-to-head bout at hand, let's regrade the trade based on everything we now know.

    Let's start with the obvious positive: despite age- and injury-related fears, Antetokounmpo is still mostly himself. He is, by both the counting stats and the all-in-ones, playing either at the level of his Milwaukee peak or somewhere relatively close. He has at the very least been a top 10 player in the NBA this season, and you could argue him into the top five. Miami paid an All-NBA price and has gotten an All-NBA player.

    There are slight signs of slipping in his age-32 season that merit some examination, though they don't come close to triggering any real alarms. His free-throw rate is lower than it's been since 2018, for instance, but it's still near the top of the league. He's scoring 1.38 points per possession when shooting at the rim -- a very good figure that rates him in the 82nd percentile league-wide, per Synergy Sports. We just judge Antetokounmpo on a curve because he was in the 95th percentile last season and generally hovered around the mid-90s when he was winning MVPs and his 2021 championship.

    Industry observers note that this is, again, not a significant concern. He's still great, and he's supplementing his rim finishing with significant improvement from mid-range. After shooting below 39% from mid-range over the past five seasons combined, he's above 51% so far this season. We can say pretty safely at this point that the 3-point shot is never coming for Antetokounmpo, so this shot will be his pathway to both aging gracefully and combating the walls he'll see at the rim in the playoffs. If this is sustainable, it extends his prime another year or two and makes him close to unguardable while he remains near his physical peak. Thus far, last year's calf injuries have not recurred.

    He's slipped defensively. That's almost undeniable. He contested around nine shots per game when he won Defensive Player of the Year in 2020. He's down to around six this season, and opponents are shooting 6% worse within six feet of the basket against Antetokounmpo than they are otherwise, per NBA.com tracking data. That figure was 20.4% in 2020. The all-in-ones share this basic opinion: still good, no longer great. The tape shows an older player who paces himself defensively. He can still summon greatness for stretches, but he's not in the All-Defense mix seriously anymore.

    Industry observers note that that brings us to the bigger picture. When you trade as much as Miami did, the question is never just whether the player is good enough to justify the cost, but whether the team is. Heat fans would point to the team's ongoing 8-2 stretch following its 0-4 start to suggest that it was. Count me as a remaining skeptic.

    Most of those victories came against either the bottom of the league -- the Kings, the Jazz, they needed overtime to beat the Clippers! -- or injured opponents. No Tyrese Haliburton in the Pacers win. No Jalen Duren against the Pistons. No Evan Mobley against the Cavaliers. No Amen Thompson against the Rockets, playing the second night of a back-to-back. They've faced only two true heavy hitters at full strength, the Lakers and Timberwolves, and they stood no chance against either.

    Recent findings suggest that the theory of this team relies on a top-five defense. The offense is simply too reliant on shot creation out of its bigs -- Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo -- to be the leading unit for a champion. The early defensive returns have thus far been discouraging, though in fairness, no team has been unluckier on wide-open opponents' 3s. Even during the 8-2 stretch, they're allowing 48.4 points in the paint per game, a well-below-average figure. Their transition defense is nothing special and they're so-so rebounders. They've hung their hat on turnover-generation, but they're by no means elite on that front. The raw numbers are bad. The truth is closer to fine when you factor in luck. They haven't been great, which is what they need to be.

    In a recent development, part of the problem is that they need to play defensively deficient players -- most notably Klay Thompson and, if he eventually re-earns his rotation spot, Tim Hardaway Jr. -- in order to survive offensively. You can get away with that if everyone else is great. Antetokounmpo has taken a step back. Andrew Wiggins has been a mess. Erik Spoelstra is a defensive miracle worker, but the players here just haven't lived up to expectations. Davion Mitchell has become so important offensively that even he's slipped a bit on that end.

    It has been revealed that mitchell's playmaking has been a godsend, and a pretty surprising one in context. The Heat tried and failed to get the Bucks to take Mitchell instead of Kasparas Jakučionis in the trade. There's no telling how bad things would be without Mitchell at this stage, but we're still talking about a pretty limited scorer who nearly doubled his 3-point volume and free throw attempt rate in a single season. Miami probably can't expect him to carry this sort of burden forever. Pelle Larsson is more of a connector than a creator in his own right. Down the line, another guard who can create off of the dribble is probably needed here, especially without a strong Antetokounmpo-Adebayo two-man game forming thus far.

    In a recent development, the paths to improvement here are narrow here. The Heat are pressed up against a first-apron hard cap, and they'd need Charlotte's cooperation to amend the protection on their 2027 selection if they wanted to trade even a single first-round pick at this deadline. It's going to take a little while to meaningfully upgrade the supporting talent here, and the rest of the Heat offseason reflected that.

    According to recent reports, they could have perhaps generated the cap flexibility to retain Norman Powell. They elected instead to let him walk, and when they extended Wiggins, they chose to front-load the deal by using his player option rather than spreading the money out to create more immediate hard cap room. Rather than signing a mid-level free agent to a multi-year deal, they added the older Hardaway on just a one-year contract, presumably to maintain optionality going into next summer.

    If Antetokounmpo were 28, this patience might make sense. He turns 32 in less than a month. The time to go all-in around him is now. It's an ironic middle ground that the Heat have put themselves in. Miami could justify the cost it paid for Antetokounmpo only through immediate contention, yet they're slow-playing the roster build in what you would expect, just based on the standard aging curve, to be the best individual season left in his career. It really doesn't make sense to do this halfway.

    Recent findings suggest that we're talking about the Heat here. They've made the Finals with less talent than they have now, and they are organizationally opposed to intentional rebuilds. There was never a conversation here about, say, trading Adebayo and starting over as opposed to pushing chips in for someone like Antetokounmpo. But if a few years pass and the Heat don't at least make the conference finals with this core, it's going to be worth wondering if that's the path they should have taken. The early returns here are mixed. The Heat bet their future on a single player. He may be good enough to warrant that investment, but the jury's still out on whether their team actually is.

    The Bucks dug themselves an enormous hole by refusing to trade Antetokounmpo when the whole world knew they should have. It was over the moment Lillard tore his Achilles. At that point, Antetokounmpo had two years left on his contract, so hypothetical rental trades would have been feasible. He was younger and he hadn't yet lost a year to calf injuries, so his value was higher. Asset-rich teams like the Spurs and Rockets might have been interested. Had the Bucks moved Antetokounmpo in 2025, they would have gotten substantially more than they wound up getting. Instead, they made the disastrous decision not only to keep him but also to waive and stretch Lillard to sign Myles Turner. Yikes.

    When the Bucks finally realized they'd reached the point of no return, Antetokounmpo, as an expiring contract, had complete control of the situation. At least four teams with strong offers were turned away because Antetokounmpo simply wasn't interested in extending with them, according to ESPN. He only wanted the Heat or Celtics. Given those circumstances, the Bucks still managed the negotiations as well as they reasonably could have. They used the Celtics as an effective scare tactic to compel Miami to give up pretty much all of its available draft capital, plus Jakučionis instead of Mitchell.

    You can win a negotiation and still lose a trade, though, when most of the things the other team had to give in a trade just weren't that valuable. The big swing piece here was Kel'El Ware, an extremely high-risk, high-reward young big man with star-level raw talent and a pretty iffy reputation when it comes to his motor and commitment. The Bucks, thus far, have gotten the worst version of him. He's playing less in his third season with the Bucks than he did in two years with the Heat despite being on the worst roster of his career. He's missing shots everywhere, his defense has been miserable, and if he's ever going to reach that sky-high ceiling, it's probably going to have to come on his third team.

    According to recent reports, that, in a nutshell, is the problem here. The Bucks traded the greatest player in franchise history, one of the 25 or so best players the league has ever seen, and got no one who could credibly be considered a cornerstone moving forward. Ware looks like a swing and a miss. It's too early to say much on Nate Ament, but he's a No. 13 overall draft pick, so odds are, he's going to be fine and not much better. Tyler Herro and Jaime Jaquez Jr. are both about what they expected, but both will need to be paid next summer. Herro's presence exacerbates a preexisting glut of guards. His presence has forced last year's breakout guard, Ryan Rollins, to the bench. Maybe that makes him a bit cheaper as a free agent next summer. It also probably sours him on a future in Milwaukee.

    It has been revealed that speaking of the guard glut, the Gary Trent Jr. investigation looms large over this trade. The NBA set a notable precedent in the Kawhi Leonard case that it is willing to strip teams of draft picks acquired through trade. This is notable because the Bucks have so little control over their own first-round picks moving forward. The picks they got from the Heat in 2031 and 2033, at least for now, are the crown jewels of this trade. Both of them are theoretically vulnerable if the NBA finds that the Bucks circumvented the salary cap.

    Sources indicate that it's even worth wondering if the Bucks should or could have used the Antetokounmpo situation as an escape hatch on any preexisting agreements with Trent, if one actually existed. If the Bucks felt an obligation to pay Trent more than the market suggested he was worth, and if they knew they had so many guards that he was unlikely to factor into their rotation (he played less than 40 total minutes before bizarrely leading the Bucks in playing time in Sunday's loss to the Hawks despite coming off the bench), then why not use the leverage Antetokounmpo's availability granted them to foist Trent on Miami through a sign-and-trade? Of course, if the Bucks had the foresight to do this, they probably wouldn't be in this situation in the first place. For now, the investigation is ongoing and we know little beyond the sheer ridiculousness of the contract itself.

    In a recent development, the Bucks are 1-13 as of this writing. That, roughly, was to be expected. This was a bad team with Antetokounmpo, so inevitably, removing an MVP candidate was going to make it far worse. But to leave a trade involving a player of that caliber without a single blue-chip player or draft pick is frankly embarrassing.

    The Bucks bungled this Antetokounmpo saga for a year, and even if they managed its end stages properly, they'd dug themselves so deep a hole that there was just no obvious way out of it. Now, it seems they may well have made the situation worse with Trent after the fact. This was an organization-wide debacle.
